title: The Traitor's Gambit
summary: The heroes are drawn into a cantina confrontation on Jakku, discover a stolen Imperial code cylinder, use it to download the coordinates of a secret prison, and break Admiral Varth out of a jungle fortress — all for the promise of a stolen fortune.

Jungle traversal — crossing gaps, climbing, rappelling. Without rope, certain routes become impossible or require much harder Athletics checks. The item everyone forgets to buy.
The Vanishing Place fortress has electronic locks, laser fences, and security panels. Without one, bypassing these is stepped down or impossible.
Generator sabotage as part of Mandrake's deal. Without proper tools, Tech actions are stepped down.
The Banshee is damaged on landing. Without a starship tool kit, all repair rolls are stepped down. Hard permission gate for getting off-world.
Multiple combats across both parts with no medical facilities. At least one is non-negotiable.
The Reestkii Landing Field read-aloud literally references macrobinoculars for recon. Also useful for jungle scouting.
Acid pools in the jungle are disguised as standing water. A tox detector identifies them without someone stepping in one.
Dim cantina, underground bunker, dense jungle canopy — multiple dark environments across both parts.
The bluff approach at the Reestkii hangar requires impersonating Imperial crew or authorized personnel.
Covering retreat across open ground during the three-way climax with Shadow Troopers flanking.
Mid-combat trauma clearance. Valuable in the multi-fight climax sequence.
Extended jungle trek. Fatigue penalties stack after 48 hours without food.
Jakku desert heat in Part 1. Environmental comfort only — no hard gate.
Coordinating with Maya for extraction timing. Encrypted channel prevents Imperial interception.

scenes.title: Bad Business at The Burning Deck
scenes.subtitle: In Media Res
scenes.readAloudPart1:
Jakku. A world the galaxy forgot... if it ever noticed. Out here on the Western Reaches, the holonet feeds are weeks old, the Republic is a memory, and the Empire is a rumor that sometimes wears a uniform. You've heard the stories filtering through the spacer lanes: whole systems pacified, Separatist holdouts burned out of their bunkers, the clone army quietly replaced by men who volunteer. The Core worlds call it order. Out here, people just call it the new way things are.

Reestkii squats on the desert flats like something the sand is trying to swallow. Drifters. Smugglers. Moisture farmers with nothing left to farm. Varga the Hutt runs what passes for an economy: debt, protection, and the quiet understanding that Imperial patrols from Arkanis Sector come through maybe twice a standard year... and they never stay.

You stepped off a rust-bucket passenger transport twelve hours ago. All of you. However you found each other, you're a crew now, or close enough to one. You eat together. You watch each other's backs. You argue about whose turn it is to pay for fuel. And right now you're waiting together, which might be the hardest part. A fixer named Cade Ryll put the word out through the spacer lanes: crew needed for a short-haul job, good pay, no questions. He named this cantina. He named a time. That was an hour ago.

The Burning Deck. That's what passes for a watering hole at the edge of civilization. The name's painted over whatever it was called before, which was painted over the name before that. Low ceiling. Failing glow-rods. The air thick with the smell of engine coolant and cheap Corellian whiskey. A Devaronian sits alone at the sabacc table in the far alcove, turning a credit chip across his knuckles. Watching everything. Playing nothing. A pair of Abyssin drifters argue in the corner booth over a rusted motivator, their guttural voices carrying even through the cantina noise. A weathered Togruta woman nurses a drink at the bar, her montrals scarred in a way that says ex-military. She hasn't looked up once, but her hand never strays far from her hip. Behind the bar, a nervous Bith wipes the same glass he's been wiping for twenty minutes, his oversized eyes flicking to the door every time the wind rattles the blast shutters.

The Burning Deck is quieter than it should be tonight. You noticed it when you docked: a Lambda-class shuttle, sitting on the landing field, flanked by two stormtroopers standing in the heat like they were carved from plastoid. Nobody docks a Lambda on Jakku without a reason. Fewer faces in the stalls on the walk in. The regulars are nursing their drinks a little harder. Talking a little softer. Something has changed the arithmetic, and nobody knows the new numbers yet.

Your drinks are warm. Your fixer is an hour late. And nothing on Jakku is going the way it was supposed to.
scenes.readAloudPart1PauseNote: PAUSE HERE. Let the players absorb the cantina. Ask: 'What do you do while you wait?' Give them time to look around, talk to each other, interact with the patrons, ask the bartender about the Imperial shuttle, or just stew. When they've had their moment — or when the energy needs a push — move to Part 2.
scenes.readAloudPart2:
The blast doors hiss open, and the heat pours in.

A young human woman. Dark hair, flight jacket, maybe twenty-five. She half-runs, half-stumbles through the entrance. One hand is pressed against her ribs, where her jacket is scorched through. She's bleeding. The Bith bartender freezes mid-wipe. The Devaronian at the sabacc table looks up for the first time all night.

She makes it four steps before her boot catches a chair leg and she pitches forward, straight into your table. Drinks scatter. Her hands hit the surface and she catches herself, breathing hard, leaving a smear of blood on the table edge. For a second she just stares at you, wild-eyed, like she's trying to decide if you're a wall, or a door.

"Sorry," she manages between breaths. Then, quieter: "Don't move."

Before anyone can ask what that means, three figures fill the entrance. A heavy-set Weequay with a scarred knuckle-duster on his right hand, and two Kyuzo in wide-brimmed war helms. Their blasters are holstered. They're not here to kill anyone. They're here to take something back. The Weequay rolls his shoulders, looks at the woman braced against your table, looks at all of you sitting around it, and makes a calculation.

"The girl took something that belongs to Varga the Hutt," he says. "This doesn't have to involve anyone else."

scenes.gmNotes:
TWO-BEAT STRUCTURE: This scene is split into two read-aloud blocks. Read Part 1 (the cantina, the crew waiting, the patrons, the atmosphere) and then PAUSE. Ask 'What do you do while you wait?' Let the players explore the room, talk to each other, interact with patrons, investigate the Imperial shuttle — whatever they want. This is their first moment in the world. Don't rush it. When the energy is right — or when they need a push — read Part 2 (Maya's entrance).

  CADE RYLL: The fixer who brought them here never shows. He's a narrative device — he gave the crew a reason to be on Jakku, at this cantina, together. Whether he got cold feet, got arrested, or got killed is up to you. If the players ask around, nobody at The Burning Deck knows the name. This is intentional — it makes them feel stranded and primes them to listen when Maya offers an alternative.

  THE PATRONS: The cantina regulars are set dressing with depth if the players engage. The Devaronian (sabacc alcove) is a small-time gambler named Siv Keel — he knows the cantina well and can tell the PCs that the Burning Deck has been tense since the Lambda landed two days ago. The Abyssin drifters are arguing over a water claim in the badlands — they're loud but harmless and can point the PCs toward the deep desert if asked. The Togruta at the bar is Nela Bren — an ex-Republic military scout who deserted after Order 66. She won't volunteer much but responds to respect; she can confirm Imperial patrols have increased in the sector. The Bith bartender, Dodd Mull, is terrified — he owes Varga money and is afraid any trouble in his establishment will bring the Hutt's people down on him. If weapons come out, the patrons scatter — most for the front entrance, a few ducking down the back hallway behind the bar.

  MAYA'S BACKSTORY (GM ONLY): Maya intercepted an Imperial Code Cylinder before Varga's operators could get their hands on it. She knew it was valuable — encrypted Imperial data, potentially worth a fortune to the right buyer. She thought she could deal with Varga: cut him in, negotiate a split, walk away clean. But Varga doesn't negotiate over things he already considers his. The cylinder was moving through his supply chain. In his eyes, she stole from him. He sent Krev's crew to recover it. They caught up to her outside the cantina — Krev put a warning shot into her ribs to slow her down. She ran anyway. The foot chase ended at The Burning Deck's blast doors.

  MAYA'S ENTRANCE: This is NOT an assassination scene. The enforcers are a retrieval crew for Varga's operation — they're here to recover the cylinder, not kill Maya. They have NOT drawn weapons inside the cantina. Maya's collision with the heroes' table looks like an accident — she tripped on a chair leg while running wounded. But the GM should know: she was already calculating. She clocked the armed crew at the table on her way in and angled toward them. The trip was real — she's hurt and off-balance — but the direction she ran was deliberate. The players should NOT know this yet. The Insight check (sc-s1-read-maya) is the gate for that information. To the players, she's just a wounded stranger who crashed into their table at the worst possible time.

  MAYA'S DIALOGUE: 'Sorry' and 'Don't move' are deliberately ambiguous. She's not explicitly asking them to play along or be her shield. She's just a hurt person trying to survive the next thirty seconds. The enforcers see her at the crew's table and make the assumption themselves — 'This doesn't have to involve anyone else' implies THEY think there might be a connection. The heroes can choose to confirm or deny that assumption.

  NARRATIVE PACING: This scene runs on narrative pacing. Do NOT call for dice unless failure forks the story. Maya crashing in — narrative. Krev's ultimatum — narrative. The bartender's nervousness — narrative. Only roll when a PC takes an action where failure has real consequences (escalation, loss of initiative, or missed intelligence).

  THE IMPERIAL SHUTTLE: Foreshadowing only. The Lambda on the landing field is not part of this scene — it seeds future tension. If players investigate during the pause, the stormtroopers say nothing. Locals don't know why it's here. Dodd the bartender nervously changes the subject. This pays off later.

  MAYA'S WOUND: Real. A blaster graze to her side — Krev's warning shot outside the cantina to slow her down during the foot chase. Non-lethal but painful and bleeding. She is desperate — genuinely — but she's also smarter than she looks.

  RESOLUTION PATHS:
  • QUICK-DRAW INTIMIDATE: A Gunslinger draws fast — blaster out before the enforcers can react. This IS the Intimidate check (Moderate), not a separate action. The draw is the statement. The blaster is leverage, not escalation. Success: Krev folds ('Not worth it today'). Failure: Krev calls the bluff ('You won't shoot over some girl you don't know') — now the PC must decide: pull the trigger (firefight) or holster (Krev smells weakness, uses Lean In).
  • SOCIAL: Charm, Deception, or Persuasion (Moderate) can convince the enforcers Maya isn't worth the trouble, redirect them, or negotiate a delay.
  • BRAWL: If anyone throws a punch, the Kyuzo respond in kind. Bar brawl — fists, headbutts, bottles. Stun damage. Blasters stay holstered.
  • FIREFIGHT: Only triggers if (a) a brawl is already happening AND someone draws a blaster, OR (b) the social check fails AND a PC with blaster already drawn refuses to hand Maya over. A drawn blaster alone is not an escalation — it's a negotiating tool. This is Star Wars.

  IF COMBAT TRIGGERS — [Join Battle] Reference:
  • Control Step-Down: Highest enemy Tier = 1 → step down Control Die 1 time
  • Failed Control (1-3): PC is surprised — [Disoriented] + [Exposed] until end of first turn
  • Mastery (8+): PC designates one enemy as surprised — [Disoriented] + [Exposed] on that NPC
  • Power Die result = initiative slot (higher acts first). NPCs act at the static Initiative shown on their stat block
  • NPC static initiative: Krev = 5, Kyuzo = 5

  Scene Tactics (NPC-agnostic — survives any NPC swap):
  • Hostiles enter through the front entrance. Expect a heavy/anchor type to push the PCs' table and lock down the social-pressure space; lighter/faster bodies will try to flank along the booth row and the alcove.
  • The center floor is the kill zone — no cover, clear sightlines. The booth row and the alcove offer light cover. The bar counter is hard cover with improvised weapons (bottles, glasses) within reach.
  • The back hallway behind the bar is the only secondary route out. The store room is a trap — full cover, no exit.
  • Door controls at the front entrance can be slammed to cut off reinforcements OR to trap the PCs inside (GM's call based on stakes).
  • Failing glow-rods make light unreliable — GMs can rule darkness/concealment tactical effects as the brawl moves.
  • Brawl rules: stun damage, improvised weapons, blasters stay holstered. If a blaster comes out, the scene shifts to lethal.
  • Bystanders scatter when weapons appear — most break for the front entrance, a few duck down the back hallway.

  KEY LORE: 15 BBY. Imperial presence on Jakku is thin — Arkanis Sector patrols, no garrison. The Lambda shuttle today is unusual and unsettling. Varga the Hutt runs the real economy here: smuggling, debt, protection. A cantina fight draws local attention (Varga's people, scavenger gangs) but NOT Imperial attention — the troopers at the landing field don't care about Hutt business.

decisionPoints.prompt: Key Decision: Bad Business at The Burning Deck

options.label: Help Maya against the enforcers
options.consequence: The heroes openly side with Maya. She remembers the moment they chose her without knowing her name. Maya joins as a trusted ally and is forthcoming about the Code Cylinder job.

options.label: Try to stay out of it
options.consequence: The enforcers assume the heroes are Maya's crew regardless — confrontation is unavoidable. Maya survives but registers the hesitation. She works with the crew but hedges, holds back intel, and watches her back.

narrativeLinks.note: Varga's enforcers here foreshadow the full encounter with his organization on Takodana.
After the brawl, Maya pulls the crew into a back booth (or out the back hallway) to make her pitch privately. Direct hand-off to Maya's Offer.

The Core worlds call it order. Out here, people just call it the new way things are.

Reestkii squats on the desert flats like something the sand is trying to swallow. Drifters. Smugglers. Moisture farmers with nothing left to farm. Varga the Hutt runs what passes for an economy: debt, protection, and the quiet understanding that Imperial patrols from Arkanis Sector come through maybe twice a standard year... and they never stay.

You stepped off a rust-bucket passenger transport twelve hours ago. All of you. However you found each other, you're a crew now, or close enough to one. You eat together. You watch each other's backs. You argue about whose turn it is to pay for fuel. And right now you're waiting together, which might be the hardest part. A fixer named Cade Ryll put the word out through the spacer lanes: crew needed for a short-haul job, good pay, no questions. He named this cantina. He named a time. That was an hour ago.

The Burning Deck. That's what passes for a watering hole at the edge of civilization. The name's painted over whatever it was called before, which was painted over the name before that. Low ceiling. Failing glow-rods. The air thick with the smell of engine coolant and cheap Corellian whiskey. A Devaronian sits alone at the sabacc table in the far alcove, turning a credit chip across his knuckles. Watching everything. Playing nothing. A pair of Abyssin drifters argue in the corner booth over a rusted motivator, their guttural voices carrying even through the cantina noise. A weathered Togruta woman nurses a drink at the bar, her montrals scarred in a way that says ex-military. She hasn't looked up once, but her hand never strays far from her hip. Behind the bar, a nervous Bith wipes the same glass he's been wiping for twenty minutes, his oversized eyes flicking to the door every time the wind rattles the blast shutters.

The Burning Deck is quieter than it should be tonight. You noticed it when you docked: a Lambda-class shuttle, sitting on the landing field, flanked by two stormtroopers standing in the heat like they were carved from plastoid. Nobody docks a Lambda on Jakku without a reason. Fewer faces in the stalls on the walk in. The regulars are nursing their drinks a little harder. Talking a little softer. Something has changed the arithmetic, and nobody knows the new numbers yet.

Your drinks are warm. Your fixer is an hour late. And nothing on Jakku is going the way it was supposed to.
encounters.tactics: PAUSE HERE after reading. Ask 'What do you do while you wait?' This is the players' first moment in the world — don't rush it. Let them explore the room, talk to each other, interact with patrons, investigate the Imperial shuttle outside. Encourage Assess actions to read the room, sus out the patrons, or check the strange Lambda. Use the GM Reference and Start Player Tutorial buttons in the header to walk a new player through the Assess mechanic if needed. Move to Beat 2 when the energy is right — or when they need a push.
encounters.gmNotes:
CADE RYLL: The fixer who brought them here never shows. He's a narrative device — he gave the crew a reason to be on Jakku, at this cantina, together. Whether he got cold feet, got arrested, or got killed is up to you. If the players ask around, nobody at The Burning Deck knows the name. This is intentional — it makes them feel stranded and primes them to listen when Maya offers an alternative.

THE PATRONS (engage if asked): The Devaronian (sabacc alcove) is Siv Keel, a small-time gambler — he can tell the PCs the cantina has been tense since the Lambda landed two days ago. The Abyssin drifters are arguing over a water claim in the badlands — loud but harmless; they can point the PCs toward the deep desert. The Togruta at the bar is Nela Bren, an ex-Republic military scout who deserted after Order 66 — she won't volunteer much but responds to respect; she can confirm Imperial patrols have increased in the sector. The Bith bartender, Dodd Mull, is terrified — he owes Varga money and is afraid any trouble will bring the Hutt's people down on him.

THE IMPERIAL SHUTTLE (foreshadowing only): The Lambda on the landing field is not part of this scene — it seeds future tension. If players investigate, the stormtroopers say nothing. Locals don't know why it's here. Dodd nervously changes the subject. This pays off later.

NARRATIVE PACING: Do NOT call for dice unless failure forks the story. Use Assess freely — it's a great low-stakes way to teach the dice system. Atmosphere and player curiosity drive this beat.

encounters.name: Beat 2 — Maya Crashes In: The Recovery
encounters.trigger: When the energy is right or the players need a push — Maya bursts through the blast doors
encounters.description: Maya half-runs, half-stumbles into the cantina, bleeding, and pitches forward into the heroes' table. Three Varga enforcers fill the doorway behind her. They want the Code Cylinder back — not blood. Heroes must decide whether to get involved. This is narrative pacing — no dice until a PC takes an action where failure matters.
encounters.readAloud:
The blast doors hiss open, and the heat pours in.

A young human woman. Dark hair, flight jacket, maybe twenty-five. She half-runs, half-stumbles through the entrance. One hand is pressed against her ribs, where her jacket is scorched through. She's bleeding. The Bith bartender freezes mid-wipe. The Devaronian at the sabacc table looks up for the first time all night.

She makes it four steps before her boot catches a chair leg and she pitches forward, straight into your table. Drinks scatter. Her hands hit the surface and she catches herself, breathing hard, leaving a smear of blood on the table edge. For a second she just stares at you, wild-eyed, like she's trying to decide if you're a wall, or a door.

"Sorry," she manages between breaths. Then, quieter: "Don't move."

Before anyone can ask what that means, three figures fill the entrance. A heavy-set Weequay with a scarred knuckle-duster on his right hand, and two Kyuzo in wide-brimmed war helms. Their blasters are holstered. They're not here to kill anyone. They're here to take something back. The Weequay rolls his shoulders, looks at the woman braced against your table, looks at all of you sitting around it, and makes a calculation.

"The girl took something that belongs to Varga the Hutt," he says. "This doesn't have to involve anyone else."
encounters.tactics: NARRATIVE TIME — no initiative, no Action+Maneuver+Exploit. Krev acts, the heroes respond. Krev steps slowly toward the table, fills the doorway with his shoulders, and lets the silence work for him. He delivers the ultimatum: stand aside, or this gets ugly. The two Kyuzo spread out behind him without a word — one drifting toward the booths, one toward the alcove — covering the room with their presence, not with drawn weapons. Krev waits. This is the heroes' choice: bribe, charm, deceive, intimidate, threaten, hand Maya over, or escalate. Krev reads the table. If they offer him an out he can take back to Varga, he takes it. If they posture without backing it up, he calls the bluff. If anyone throws a punch or draws a blaster with intent to use it, advance to Beat 3 and roll Join Battle.
encounters.gmNotes:
NARRATIVE TIME, NOT COMBAT: This whole beat runs on narrative pacing. Nobody has an Action / Maneuver / Exploit budget yet — those only exist once Beat 3 starts and you roll Join Battle. Heroes describe what they do; if it matters, call for a single check. Krev and the Kyuzo simply act and let the heroes react.

MAYA'S BACKSTORY (GM ONLY): Maya intercepted an Imperial Code Cylinder before Varga's operators could get their hands on it. She thought she could deal with Varga: cut him in, negotiate a split, walk away clean. But Varga doesn't negotiate over things he already considers his. He sent Krev's crew to recover it. Krev put a warning shot into her ribs to slow her down. She ran anyway. The foot chase ended at The Burning Deck's blast doors.

MAYA'S ENTRANCE: This is NOT an assassination scene. The enforcers are a retrieval crew — they're here to recover the cylinder, not kill Maya. They have NOT drawn weapons inside the cantina. Maya's collision with the heroes' table looks like an accident. But the GM should know: she clocked the armed crew on her way in and angled toward them. The trip was real — she's hurt — but the direction she ran was deliberate. The players should NOT know this yet. The Insight check (sc-s1-read-maya) is the gate for that information.

MAYA'S DIALOGUE: 'Sorry' and 'Don't move' are deliberately ambiguous. She's not explicitly asking them to play along. The enforcers see her at the crew's table and make the assumption themselves — 'This doesn't have to involve anyone else' implies THEY think there might be a connection. The heroes can choose to confirm or deny that assumption.

MAYA'S WOUND: Real. A blaster graze to her side. Non-lethal but painful and bleeding. She is desperate — genuinely — but she's also smarter than she looks.

HOW HEROES CAN RESPOND: Resolve player options through the Checks for this Scene strip — Insight (read Maya), Charm, Deception, or Intimidate (face Krev). Hand her over ends the scene; an attack jumps to Beat 3.

ESCALATION TO BEAT 3 — only on these triggers:
• Anyone throws the first punch (brawl).
• A blaster is fired, or drawn AND clearly committed to use (firefight).
• Social attempt fails AND the heroes still refuse to back down or hand her over.

encounters.name: Beat 3 — Things Got Loud: Cantina Brawl
encounters.trigger: Only if someone throws the first punch, or social resolution fails badly and PCs refuse to back down
encounters.description: Bar brawl in a cramped cantina. Fists, headbutts, thrown bottles, overturned tables. Stun damage — no one is trying to kill. Blasters stay holstered. Combat only escalates to lethal if: (a) a brawl is already happening AND someone draws a blaster, OR (b) social failed AND a PC with blaster drawn refuses to hand Maya over. [map:burning-deck]
encounters.readAloud:
Whatever just happened — a punch, a drawn blaster, a shouted ultimatum — the air in The Burning Deck snaps tight. Krev's eyes narrow. The Kyuzo on his left rolls his shoulders inside that wide war helm. The Bith dives behind the bar. Chairs scrape across the floor as the regulars decide, all at once, that they would rather be anywhere else. Maya pushes off your table, blood smearing the edge, and finds whatever cover she can.

The Weequay smiles — slow and unhappy.

"Fine. We do it the loud way."

Launch the encounter here: [encounter:enc-s1-brawl]
encounters.tactics: SCENE TACTICS (NPC-agnostic — applies to whatever enforcers the GM uses): The cantina is a cramped one-room interior. The center floor is open with no cover; the booth row and the alcove offer light cover; the bar counter is hard cover with improvised weapons (bottles, glasses, chairs). Three hostiles enter through the front entrance — expect a heavy front-and-center to lock the PCs' table, with lighter/faster bodies trying to flank along the booth row and the alcove. Anyone caught on the center floor is exposed. The back hallway behind the bar is the only secondary route out; the store room is full cover but a trap (no exit). Failing glow-rods make light unreliable — GMs can rule darkness/concealment tactical effects as the brawl moves. If the fight stays unarmed, it's stun damage and improvised weapons. If a blaster comes out, the scene shifts to lethal — bystanders scatter for the entrance, a few for the back hallway.
encounters.gmNotes:
[Join Battle] REFERENCE:
• Control Step-Down: Highest enemy Tier = 1 → step down Control Die 1 time
• Failed Control (1-3): PC is surprised — [Disoriented] + [Exposed] until end of first turn
• Mastery (8+): PC designates one enemy as surprised — [Disoriented] + [Exposed] on that NPC
• Power Die result = initiative slot (higher acts first). NPCs act at the static Initiative shown on their stat block
• NPC static initiative: Krev = 5, Kyuzo = 5

NPC TACTICS:
• KREV (Anchor / Martial, Standard, Tier 1): No maneuver. Moves into the PCs' table and uses Shield Slam (Physique vs Dodge/Endure) with his Combat Gloves. Power options: Shove Back (push target 1 zone, peels a brawler off Maya) or Defensive Posture ([Guarded 1] when surrounded). Intercept exploit: he becomes the target of any attack aimed at an ally in his zone — use it to shield the Kyuzo. Hardened passive: +1 Defense in Physique. Backup attacks: Haymaker (Physique), Blastem (Reflex) only if lethal.
• KYUZO SKIRMISHERS ×2 (Harrier / Martial, Minion, Tier 1): No maneuver. Swift passive grants +1 zone on Move — each one reaches the booth row or the alcove in a single Move. Action is Blindside (Physique vs Dodge/Endure), strongest from a flank. Power options: Hamstring ([Slowed]) to pin a fleeing target, or Expose Flank to strip cover and set up Krev. Pursuit exploit: follow a target out of zone for free with no Opening. Minions — one solid hit drops each.

KEY LORE: 15 BBY. Imperial presence on Jakku is thin. A cantina fight draws local attention (Varga's people, scavenger gangs) but NOT Imperial attention — the troopers at the landing field don't care about Hutt business.

ALL PATRONS scatter when weapons come out — most break for the front entrance, a few duck down the back hallway behind the bar.

composition.positioning: Krev fills the entrance with the two Kyuzo at his shoulders. Once the standoff begins, the Kyuzo use their Swift passive to silently Move to the booth row and the alcove, cutting off the PCs' table from both sides.

environmentMechanics.name: Dim Cantina Lighting
environmentMechanics.effect: Failing glow-rods create shadow pools. Ranged attacks at distance stepped down.
environmentMechanics.mitigation: Close range unaffected. Rodian infrared / Sullustan darkvision ignore penalty.

environmentMechanics.name: Cantina Furniture
environmentMechanics.effect: Overturned tables = light cover. Bar = hard cover. Chairs and bottles as improvised weapons.
environmentMechanics.mitigation: Athletics check to flip a table for instant cover.

environmentMechanics.name: Panicking Patrons
environmentMechanics.effect: Civilians scramble for exits. Ranged attacks into crowds risk bystanders.
environmentMechanics.mitigation: Careful shot placement or waiting for clear lines.

zones.label: Solid Wall
zones.terrain: Duracrete wall. Impassable. Channels all traffic through B1/C1 entrance.

zones.label: Entrance (West)
zones.terrain: Blast door entrance. Jakku sunlight pours in. No cover — anyone standing here is fully exposed. Door controls on the wall.

zones.label: Entrance (East)
zones.terrain: Blast door entrance. Wide enough for three abreast. No cover. The glare from outside imposes no penalty but is narratively blinding.

zones.label: Solid Wall
zones.terrain: Duracrete wall. Impassable. Storage crates stacked against the outside.

zones.label: Booth Row
zones.terrain: Curved booth seating along the wall. Light cover from booth backs. Shadow pool — dim lighting penalty applies to ranged attacks targeting or from this zone at range. A few patrons nursing drinks.

zones.label: Center Floor (PCs' Table)
zones.terrain: The heroes' table. Light cover from furniture. A PC can use Find Cover (maneuver) to flip the table for improved light cover. Central position — adjacent to all Row 2 and Row 1/3 zones. This is where the action starts.

zones.label: Open Floor
zones.terrain: Open cantina floor. No cover, no obstacles. Clear sightlines to every other zone. The kill zone if blasters come out.

zones.label: Alcove
zones.terrain: Recessed alcove with a sabacc table. Light cover from the table edge. Deep shadow — dim lighting penalty applies. A patron or two hiding here.

zones.label: Back Hallway
zones.terrain: Narrow corridor to the back exit. No cover. Leads to the alley behind the cantina — the escape route. Dim lighting from a single failing glow-rod.

zones.label: Bar (West)
zones.terrain: West end of the bar counter. Hard cover — the bar is solid durasteel and wood. Bottles and glasses as improvised weapons (Light chassis, stun). The bartender's position. Maya flees here if combat starts.

zones.label: Bar (East)
zones.terrain: East end of the bar counter. Hard cover. Tap system and storage underneath. Same improvised weapon access as B3. Good defensive position with sightlines to the entrance.

zones.label: Store Room
zones.terrain: Closed door (requires maneuver to open). Full cover once inside. Dark — no light source. Crates of supplies, kegs. Dead end — defensible but no exit. A cornered position.

startingPositions.notes: Seated at their table. Central position with light cover.
Crashes into the dining area. Flees to the bar (hard cover) if combat starts.
Enters through blast doors. Exposed — no cover. Moves into the PCs' table to threaten with Shield Slam.
Behind Krev at the entrance. Moves to the booth row (Swift passive) to flank the PCs' table.
Flanking the entrance. Moves to the alcove (Swift passive) to cut off the far side of the PCs' table.
Scattered across booths. Flee to entrance or back hallway if weapons are drawn.

tacticalMap.gmTacticalNotes:
SCENE-LEVEL TACTICAL NOTES (NPC-agnostic — applies to whatever enforcers the GM uses):

• STARTING POSTURE: The lead enforcer enters through the front entrance and stays exposed there — collectors expect compliance, not a fight. The supporting hostiles fan out during the social phase, sliding silently into the booth row and the alcove to flank the PCs' table on both sides. This is positioning, not aggression — the social pressure is the weapon.

• IF COMBAT TRIGGERS: Hostiles push the center floor toward the PCs' table for melee range. Flankers attack from the booth row and alcove they pre-positioned in. The open floor between the entrance and the PCs' table is the kill zone — no cover, clear sightlines. The booth row and alcove offer light cover for whoever holds them. The bar counter is the strongest defensive position (hard cover, improvised weapons within reach).

• ESCAPE ROUTES: The back hallway behind the bar is the only secondary route out. The store room is a trap — full cover, no exit. The front entrance becomes contested as soon as combat starts.

• ENVIRONMENT LEVERAGE: Door controls at the front entrance can cut off reinforcements OR trap PCs inside. Bottles, glasses, and chairs are improvised weapons accessible from the bar and booth row. Failing glow-rods make light unreliable — GM may rule darkness/concealment effects as the brawl moves through the room.

intel: Varga the Hutt sent a retrieval crew — this cylinder is worth something to him
The thugs were recovery, not assassination — Varga wants the item, not blood

pacing.openingBeat: Part 1 establishes Jakku, the crew's identity, the missing fixer, and the subdued cantina. Players get time to explore the room and its patrons. The pause gives them ownership of the space before the plot arrives.
pacing.risingAction: Part 2 — Maya crashes in wounded. Thugs fill the doorway. Krev delivers his ultimatum. Kyuzo silently flank. The crew must decide whether this stranger's problem is their problem.
pacing.climax: The decision — fast-draw intimidate, social play, or let it go to fists. One roll that matters.
pacing.resolution: The fight is done. The cantina is wrecked. The thugs are gone — one way or another. Maya is still here, bleeding at the table, watching you with an expression that is not quite gratitude.

disciplineChallenges.context: Reading Maya — is that collision really an accident? Only roll if a PC specifically says they're trying to read her. Failure matters: it hides that she angled toward their table on purpose, which colors trust going forward.
disciplineChallenges.narrativePacing: Roll only if asked. Do not prompt for this check.

control.failure: Maya reads as a desperate woman who tripped at the worst possible moment. Pure bad luck. No indication she chose their table — which she did.
control.mastery: The PC also catches something in the half-second before Maya 'tripped' — her eyes were already on their table. She tracked them before the fall. She's sharper than she's letting on, and this whole collision was a lot less accidental than it looked.

effect.fleeting: The wound is real. The fear is real. But there's something about the angle of her fall — she didn't stumble randomly. She was heading toward this table.
effect.masterful: She chose this table. She saw armed people and made a calculation mid-sprint. The trip was real — she's genuinely hurt — but the direction was tactical.
effect.legendary: All of the above, plus: her injuries are from a warning shot, not a real attempt to kill. Whoever shot her wanted to slow her down, not put her down. This is a retrieval job, not a hit. And that 'Don't move' wasn't panic — it was an instruction.

disciplineChallenges.context: The Gunslinger's fast draw IS this check — blaster out before the enforcers can react. The draw is the statement, the blaster is leverage. Other vocations can use presence, posture, or reputation. This is the ONE roll that determines whether violence happens.
disciplineChallenges.narrativePacing: This is a story fork. Always roll.

control.failure: Krev doesn't flinch. 'You won't shoot over some girl you don't know.' The PC must decide: pull the trigger (firefight) or holster it (Krev uses Lean In, smells weakness, pressure escalates).
control.mastery: The draw is so fast that one Kyuzo involuntarily steps back. Krev's crew is shaken — even if Krev holds, his backup has lost confidence.

effect.fleeting: Krev pauses. He's recalculating but hasn't decided to leave. 'Varga's going to hear about this.' Buys time but doesn't resolve — a second social action may be needed.
effect.masterful: 'Not worth it today.' Krev withdraws with the Kyuzo. Warns that Varga remembers faces. Clean resolution — no combat.
effect.legendary: Krev folds immediately and drops intel on the way out: 'Varga's got bigger problems than some cylinder — something about an Imperial deal gone wrong.' Seeds future plot threads.

disciplineChallenges.context: Talking the enforcers down or redirecting them. Appealing to Krev's professionalism — he's a retrieval man, not a killer. Failure matters: escalation.
disciplineChallenges.narrativePacing: Story fork. Always roll.

control.failure: Krev sees through it. 'Nice try. Hand her over.' Social approach has failed — next move is violence or surrender.
control.mastery: The ease under pressure lands before Krev can even respond — one of the Kyuzo bodyguards visibly shifts his weight back, disengaging before the boss gives the order. Even if Krev holds firm, his backup has already made their calculation.

effect.fleeting: Krev hesitates — he's listening, but not convinced. He'll give one more chance to make a real offer. A second social action can close this.
effect.masterful: Thugs are mollified or confused enough to withdraw. Krev leaves muttering but doesn't escalate.
effect.legendary: Krev is genuinely charmed. Leaves on almost-friendly terms. 'You're smooth. Tell the girl Varga's patience isn't infinite, but today she gets a pass.'

disciplineChallenges.context: Claiming Maya already handed the cylinder off, or that there's a bigger play in motion. Selling a lie to a professional enforcer. Failure matters: escalation.
disciplineChallenges.narrativePacing: Story fork. Always roll.

control.failure: 'I know everyone who moves product for Varga. You're nobody.' The lie collapses. Krev's suspicion is now active hostility.
control.mastery: Krev not only swallows the lie clean — he volunteers something on the way out. An offhand comment about Varga being distracted by 'Imperial trouble at the docks' confirms the lie landed completely and plants a thread the PCs didn't ask for.

effect.fleeting: Krev hesitates — the story doesn't quite add up but he can't immediately disprove it. He'll leave to verify, buying the PCs time but not resolving the situation permanently.
effect.masterful: Krev buys it. Leaves to confirm with his boss. By the time he realizes the deception, the PCs are long gone.
effect.legendary: Krev completely buys it and offers an apology. 'Didn't know she had people. Tell your boss we're square.' The PCs have created a false paper trail that could be useful later.

scenes.title: Maya's Offer
scenes.subtitle: The Short Rest
scenes.readAloudPart1:
Nobody says anything. You move.

Maya is already on her feet — one hand pressed to her ribs, the other waving you forward. The Bith bartender doesn't try to stop you. Neither does anyone else.

Three blocks from The Burning Deck, down a service alley that smells of recycled coolant and old grease, she pushes open the rusted shutter of a derelict vaporator maintenance shed. Inside: a collapsed workbench, a tangle of stripped conduit, half a moisture collector that hasn't moved in years. No windows. One way in.

She pulls the shutter closed behind you and sinks against the wall. A breath. The first real one she's taken since she hit your table.

"Give me a minute."
scenes.readAloudPart1PauseNote: This is the short rest. Give the party a moment to settle. Someone may want to treat her wound (Medicine). Someone may want to read her while her guard is down (Insight). Let the room breathe before she makes her pitch.
scenes.readAloudPart2:
She reaches into her jacket — carefully, given the state of her ribs — and produces a dull metallic cylinder about the length of a stylus. Sets it on the bench between you.

"Imperial Code Cylinder. Encrypted. I pulled it out of Varga's supply chain before his people knew what they had. I don't know exactly what's on it — but I know it's worth something to the right buyer. The problem is, I can't decrypt it."

She looks around the group. Taking her time. Like she's still deciding something.

"There's a droid out in the badlands. Switch. He can crack anything. I need people who can handle themselves." A beat. "You just proved you can."

She holds up one hand, fingers spread.

"Ten shares. One each for your crew. Five for me." Her hand stays up. "I have the ship. I have the score. And right now, none of us have anything better to do."
scenes.gmNotes:
SHORT REST: The party has cleared the cantina and gone to ground. The derelict vaporator shed gives them cover — one entrance, no sight lines from the street, and enough time to breathe before Varga's people figure out where they went. This is a short rest window. Allow recovery actions. The clock is running but it isn't urgent yet.

MAYA'S CONDITION: Maya is carrying [Debilitated Physique ×2] from the blaster graze. This is a real mechanical state — it limits what she can do physically in future scenes until cleared. She won't ask for help. If someone offers medicine, she accepts without ceremony. Track how many points are cleared — it affects her participation going forward.

MAYA'S READ: She does NOT know who the party was waiting for. She spotted them from across the cantina when she came through the door — armed crew, professional posture, waiting for someone who hadn't shown. She made a calculation and aimed for their table. The trip was real. The direction was tactical. She chose them by read, not by intelligence.

THE PITCH: Maya's opening offer is 10 shares total — 1 for each member of the crew, 5 for herself. She frames it plainly: she has the ship, she has the score, and the cylinder might be worth nothing. That's the risk everyone is taking. She does NOT explain exactly how she got the cylinder. If pressed: 'Does it matter? It's here. They want it back. That's all you need to know.'

THE SHARES SYSTEM: Maya opens at 5 shares for herself. Persuasion can reduce her share to a minimum of 2 — she will not go lower. Each share removed from her increases the relative value of everyone else's cut. If the players don't push, she holds at 5 and doesn't resent it. If they push well, she respects it.

IF THEY REFUSE: Maya goes to Switch alone. The PCs can still learn about Switch from the cantina contacts (the Abyssin drifters know the badlands, Nela Bren knows Switch by reputation) — but they lose their cut and Maya's trust. This should feel like a missed opportunity, not a wall.

npcs.name: Maya
npcs.notes: Solo smuggler. Carrying [Debilitated Physique ×2] from the blaster graze — a real mechanical condition that limits her physical capability in future scenes until treated. She chose this crew by read, not prior knowledge. The trip into their table was real; the direction was deliberate.
npcs.behavior: Direct and transactional. No begging, no sob story. She reads the room — appeals to greed for mercenaries, self-interest for investigators, practicality for everyone else. She does NOT know who the party was waiting for. She does NOT volunteer personal history. Deflects questions about how she got the cylinder.
dialogue: "Imperial Code Cylinder. Encrypted. I pulled it out of Varga's supply chain before his people knew what they had."
"There's a droid out in the badlands — Switch. He can crack anything. I need people who can handle themselves. You just proved you can."
"Ten shares. One each for your crew. Five for me. I have the ship and the score."
"The cylinder might be worth a fortune. It might be worth nothing. I'm betting it's the former. You're welcome to bet with me."
"Does it matter how I got it? It's here. They want it back. That's all you need to know."
npcs.intel: Maya intercepted an encrypted Imperial Code Cylinder from Varga's supply chain. She needs it decrypted by Switch, a droid information broker hidden in the badlands. She is offering 10 shares — 1 per crew member, 5 for herself — with a floor of 2 shares for herself if negotiated down.
npcs.nonCombatNote: No threatBuild required: this scene is a private conversation. Maya does not fight here. Her combat statblock (used only if a fight unexpectedly breaks out — e.g. on the Banshee in P2-S1) is carried on her P1-S1 entry and reused there.

scenes.hazards: Derelict vaporator maintenance shed. Rusted shutter, unstable floor sections, exposed conduit. Varga's people don't know where the party went — but that window won't last.

options.label: Accept Maya's offer at her terms — 5 shares for her
options.consequence: The deal is done. The party heads into the badlands with Maya. Scene 3 (The Processor) follows directly.

options.label: Negotiate for a better split (Persuasion)
options.consequence: Maya's share can be reduced to a minimum of 2. Each tier of success drops her share by one. She respects the play if it's done well.

options.label: Demand more information before committing
options.consequence: Maya gives what she can but holds back personal details. Insight reveals her real motives. She won't wait indefinitely — they need to move.

options.label: Refuse and let Maya go alone
options.consequence: Maya leaves. PCs can still find Switch through cantina contacts (Abyssin drifters know the badlands, Nela Bren knows Switch by reputation) — but they lose their cut and Maya's trust.

options.label: Try to take the cylinder from Maya
options.consequence: Maya is wounded but not cornered. She'll bolt. The cylinder leads nowhere without Switch — and the PCs have made an enemy of their best lead.

narrativeLinks.note: If the crew accepts Maya's offer, she leads them to Switch's bunker in the Sinkhole — a speeder ride into the badlands. If they refuse, the adventure stalls; offer Cade Ryll never showing as the nudge back in.

disciplineChallenges.context: Treating Maya's blaster graze during the short rest. control.failure: Maya is hard to read. She's competent, wounded, and deliberate. Beyond that — nothing surfaces.
control.mastery: The PC also catches how Maya chooses to sit — weight away from the door, back to the wall, sightlines on the shutter. She has been in rooms like this before. Not Varga's rooms. Rooms people run to, not from.

effect.fleeting: She's not desperate — she's running a calculated play. The fear is real but controlled. She needs backup because the alternative is worse, not because she has no other options.
effect.masterful: She chose this crew deliberately. She spotted them from across the cantina — armed, waiting, professional — and made a decision before she hit their table. The cylinder is real. The pitch is genuine. But she has been evaluating them since she walked through the door.
effect.legendary: Maya knows more about what is on the cylinder than she is admitting. She did not just stumble across it in Varga's supply chain — she went looking for it specifically. Whatever is on that device, she already has a theory. And she is afraid of being right.

disciplineChallenges.context: Negotiating Maya's share of the score. She opens at 5 shares for herself — she has the ship, the score, and the cylinder might be worth nothing. effect.legendary: Maya drops to 2 shares — her floor. "Don't push it further." But she says it like someone who respects what just happened.

scenes.title: The Processor
scenes.gmNotes:
Switch is a crime lord and information broker, not an ally — he is a businessman. He examines the code cylinder and quotes a diagnostic fee the heroes can't afford. He then offers a deal: reduced fee in exchange for the heroes becoming information assets for his network. As they travel, they pass along intel — names, locations, movements, deals. If the intel is validated and leads to actionable resources, Switch compensates them. He also serves as a black market connection for gear, smuggling contacts, and fencing stolen goods.

The decryption reveals: the cylinder is an Imperial ghost transfer authorization device. It does NOT contain location data or vault coordinates. What it CAN do is authenticate into Imperial shuttle nav systems — essentially a master key for accessing flight computers on Imperial shuttles.

After the reveal, Maya connects the dots: she's been watching an Imperial Lambda-class shuttle sitting on the Reestkii Landing Field. If the cylinder can get them into the shuttle's nav computer, they can download its flight logs and destination data — which could lead to Varth and the fortune.

Switch should feel dangerous and calculating despite his droid body. His deal is transactional but honest.

"I reduce my fee. In exchange, you become assets in my intelligence network. You travel, you observe, you report. Validated intel earns compensation. Think of it as... mutually beneficial employment."

"Ghost transfer authorization. Military grade. This cylinder authenticates into Imperial shuttle nav computers — flight logs, destination data, everything in the system. Someone wanted access to Imperial movements."

It does not contain location data directly, but can access flight computers on Imperial vessels. He offers a deal: reduced diagnostic fee in exchange for the heroes becoming recurring information assets for his network.

disciplineChallenges.context: Negotiating Switch's terms for a better deal on the information asset arrangement. Switch is [Transactional] — he responds to value, not pressure. A well-structured argument can move him; flattery cannot.
disciplineChallenges.narrativePacing: Roll only if the PCs push for better terms. Switch's default offer is fair — don't pressure players to negotiate if they accept.

control.failure: Standard terms stand — reduced fee, no advance. Switch is unmoved. 'The offer is what it is.'
control.mastery: The PC structures the argument so precisely that Switch pauses mid-breath — not a hesitation, a recalculation. He notes it. Whatever he concludes about this crew, they've upgraded in his estimation.

effect.fleeting: Minor concession — Switch throws in a local intel data chip as a sweetener. Not a change to the core terms, but an acknowledgment.
effect.masterful: Switch improves the deal — offers a modest advance on future validated intel value. He's decided they're worth investing in slightly.
effect.legendary: Switch offers true partnership terms — ongoing reciprocal intelligence sharing, not just one-directional asset work. 'You bring me good product, I bring you things you didn't know you needed.' A droid broker in their pocket.

disciplineChallenges.context: Reading Switch's motives. What does this droid actually want — and why does he want it so fast?
disciplineChallenges.narrativePacing: Roll only if a player specifically tries to read him. Droid body language is a different read than organic.

control.failure: Switch is inscrutable. Photoreceptors, calibrated tone, deliberate stillness — nothing surfaces.
control.mastery: The PC catches something in how Switch positions himself relative to the cylinder — a slight lean away from it, like it's something he wants out of his shop as fast as possible. He's not neutral. He's motivated.

effect.fleeting: Switch is genuinely interested in the cylinder — this is business, not a trap. He wants it analyzed and gone.
effect.masterful: Switch is building a network of obligations across the Outer Rim. He's not just a broker — he's positioning himself as the indispensable middleman. This deal is one thread in a much larger web.
effect.legendary: Switch is afraid of this cylinder specifically. Not of the PCs, not of Varga. Of what's on that device and who will come looking once it surfaces. He wants the PCs to succeed because success gets a dangerous asset far away from his bunker.

disciplineChallenges.context: Examining the cylinder data directly after Switch's analysis — looking for details the droid's summary may have glossed over.
disciplineChallenges.narrativePacing: Optional. Rewards curiosity. Roll only if a player digs in.

control.failure: The data is dense Imperial encryption. Without specialist knowledge the analysis reads as straightforward authorization protocols.
control.mastery: The PC notices the data structure before reading the content — the format itself is irregular. This cylinder was authored by someone who knew Imperial encryption protocols from the inside. Not someone with access. Someone who wrote the spec.

effect.fleeting: The authorization codes are military-grade, not civilian. This cylinder came from someone with significant clearance.
effect.masterful: The authorization codes reference routing designations connected to 'Project Leviathan' — a name that doesn't appear in any public Imperial registry.
effect.legendary: The cylinder carries a ghost layer — hidden metadata showing it was deliberately copied, not stolen in transit. Someone inside the Imperial apparatus wanted this device to leave the facility. This was a plant, not a theft.

disciplineChallenges.context: Verifying Switch's analysis is genuine and complete — did the droid give them everything, or is he holding a partition back?
disciplineChallenges.narrativePacing: Optional. Trust verification for suspicious players.

control.failure: No way to independently verify without comparable equipment. The outputs look legitimate but that's all you can confirm.
control.mastery: The PC notices Switch's equipment has already run a secondary sweep he hasn't mentioned. The results sit in a partition he didn't open during the briefing. He gave them everything they asked for — but there's more he didn't volunteer.

effect.fleeting: The analysis appears complete and unaltered on surface review. No obvious signs of tampering or selective output.
effect.masterful: Analysis is genuine. Switch delivered everything his equipment surfaced. Whatever he knows, he shared it.
effect.legendary: Analysis is complete — AND the secondary partition is accessible with the right credentials. The cylinder has a second layer Switch didn't mention. It requires a different authentication to open. That key isn't here.

scenes.readAloudPart1:
Maya leads you out of the settlement and into the open desert. The sun hammers down as you cross a dry wash and climb through a field of broken mesas — wind-carved rock pillars standing like the ribs of something ancient. No tracks. No markers. Nothing out here but heat and silence and the whisper of sand moving against itself.

Maya moves with purpose. She knows this path.
scenes.readAloudPart1PauseNote: Let the players take in the desert. If anyone wants to scout or investigate the surroundings, this is the moment. Ask: "What do you notice as you walk?" or "Are you watching for anything specific?" Then move to Part 2 when they reach the bunker.
scenes.readAloudPart2:
The sinkhole opens without warning — a ragged crater in the mesa floor, maybe thirty meters across, its walls carved smooth by millennia of wind. At the bottom, half-buried in sand, sits what looks like an abandoned moisture vaporator station. Maya slides down the slope and keys in a code on a rusted panel. A blast door grinds open.

Inside is a technological cave — wires hang from the ceiling like vines, the floor is a carpet of droid parts and discarded components. Screens flicker with data feeds from across the sector. But in the center of the filth sits a pristine, priceless desk of Japor ivory wood — polished to a mirror shine, completely out of place in this desert hole.

Behind it, a protocol droid who has clearly forgone memory wipes for decades regards you with an unsettling intelligence. His photoreceptors track each of you individually as you enter.

"Ah. Maya. You brought friends." The droid's vocabulator carries the precise, faintly condescending tone of old Republic diplomatic programming. "How unlike you."

scenes.title: The Gangster's Revenge
scenes.readAloud:
The bunker's motion sensors scream. Before you can react, the hatch above explodes inward. Standing in the smoking frame is a massive Chevin — Ganga Lor, Varga the Hutt's lieutenant. His trunk curls with fury as he levels a heavy blaster at the room.

"Nobody steals from the Mighty Varga," he growls, his voice like grinding stone. "Not the girl. Not the droid. And definitely not you."
scenes.gmNotes:
Ganga Lor wants to recover the code cylinder and make an example of everyone involved. Varga wants the cylinder because it could lead someone to Varth before Varga gets to him — Varga needs Varth alive to unlock the encrypted account in his own financial network.

The fight takes place in cramped quarters — use the environment: toppling droid part stacks, shooting steam pipes, activating Switch's security turrets. This is a significant combat — Ganga Lor is a real threat.

GANGA LOR IS KILLED IN THIS FIGHT. This is a mandatory outcome. He does not escape or retreat. His death establishes that the heroes' actions have real consequences and removes Varga's local enforcer from the board.

After the fight, if the deal with Switch was struck earlier, Switch finishes the cylinder analysis and delivers the ghost transfer authorization reveal. If the analysis was already complete, the fight simply confirms that Varga is actively hunting the cylinder.

scenes.title: The Heist
scenes.readAloud:
The Reestkii Landing Field stretches out in the heat haze — a militarized zone on the outskirts of the settlement. Through your macrobinoculars, you see it: a Lambda-class Imperial shuttle sitting on the landing pad, flanked by stormtroopers in transition-era armor, dirty from the desert but standing sharp.

The shuttle's nav computer holds the answers — flight logs, destination data, coordinates. But the cylinder only works at the terminal. You have to get inside the shuttle, plug in, authenticate, and download before anyone notices you don't belong here.

The clock is ticking. Imperial pickup crews rotate on a schedule, and the next shift change is less than an hour out.
scenes.gmNotes:
This is the heroes' first brush with the Young Empire. The target is the Lambda shuttle's nav computer. The heroes must physically reach the shuttle, use the code cylinder to authenticate into the flight computer, and download the destination coordinates — which reveal the Vanishing Place on Ajan Kloss, where Admiral Varth is being held.

OPTIONS:
• BLUFF: Impersonate Imperial crew or authorized maintenance personnel. Disguise Kit helps. Deception check (Moderate) to approach without suspicion.
• STEALTH: Sneak through maintenance areas or use terrain cover to reach the shuttle unseen. Stealth/Skulduggery (Moderate).
• DISTRACTION: Create a diversion to draw the guards away. Tech, Deception, or creative approaches (Moderate).
• DIRECT ASSAULT: Possible but loud. Brings reinforcements quickly. Not recommended but not forbidden.

THE DOWNLOAD: Once at the shuttle's flight computer, a Tech check (Easy with the cylinder, Moderate without) accesses the nav logs. The coordinates point to the jungle moon of Ajan Kloss — a location labeled 'The Vanishing Place' in Imperial records. A successful Investigation check on the data reveals references to 'Project Leviathan' in the shipping metadata.

EXTRACTION: Once the download is complete (or the alarm is raised), the heroes must escape the landing field. Maya has the Banshee prepped at a secondary pad. The escape from Jakku transitions directly into Part 2.

IMPORTANT: The code cylinder is effectively dead after use. The authentication codes will be flagged and disabled by Imperial security within hours.

GROUP CHALLENGE: This scene uses a Victory Point (VP) accumulation mechanic. The crew plans and executes the infiltration of Reestkii Landing Field as a coordinated team effort. Each PC picks a discipline and describes their approach — stealth, deception, tech, investigation, piloting, or charm.

MECHANICS:
- Tier 1 / Power 4 across all disciplines
- Each PC rolls Control (stepped down 1 die for T1). Control 4+ = success.
- On success, roll Power vs P4 to determine effect tier:
  • Fleeting (Power loses or ties) = 1 VP
  • Masterful (Power wins) = 2 VP
  • Legendary (Power wins decisively) = 3 VP
  • Mastery (Control 8+) = +1 VP added to the tier result
- 12 VP total = ghost run, clean infiltration and extraction
- Below 12, they can attempt more rolls or proceed with partial stealth compromised

FAILURE CONSEQUENCE: A failed Control roll (below 4) means the alarm triggers. Stormtroopers lock down the perimeter, reinforcements scramble, and every subsequent action is stepped up in difficulty. Maya reports troop movement near the Banshee.

VP THRESHOLDS — Read aloud or paraphrase at each threshold:

3 VP: Perimeter gap identified — maintenance gate on the south side, shielded by cargo containers.

6 VP: Jurisdictional friction exploitable — three-minute shift overlap window where nobody watches the ramp.

9 VP: External access panel unlocked — slicer can patch in from outside, halving time inside the shuttle.

11 VP: Fuel tanker crossing creates a ninety-second sightline block from the guard tower.

12 VP: Ghost run. No alarms, no detection, no trace. The Empire won't know until the next diagnostic cycle.

groupChallenge.name: Infiltrating Reestkii Landing Field
groupChallenge.description: The crew plans and executes an infiltration of the Imperial-controlled Reestkii Landing Field to reach the Lambda shuttle's nav computer. Each PC contributes a different angle — distraction, disguise, technical bypass, scouting — to get the team inside, download the coordinates, and get out before the alarm brings the full garrison down on them.
groupChallenge.failureConsequence: The alarm triggers. Stormtroopers lock down the perimeter and reinforcements scramble from the garrison barracks. The crew's window to reach the shuttle shrinks to minutes. Every subsequent action at the landing field is stepped up in difficulty, and Maya radios that she's seeing troop movement near the Banshee's secondary pad.

thresholds.intel: The perimeter has a gap — a maintenance access gate on the south side, shielded from the guard tower's line of sight by stacked cargo containers. It's not locked, just latched.

The stormtroopers and Warlord's guards don't coordinate. There's a three-minute window during shift overlap where neither group is watching the shuttle's boarding ramp. The jurisdictional friction is exploitable.

The shuttle's external access panel is unlocked — the maintenance crew left it open after their last diagnostic. A slicer can patch into the nav computer from outside the cockpit, cutting the time inside the shuttle in half.
A fuel tanker is scheduled to cross the tarmac in twelve minutes. Its path blocks the guard tower's sightline to the shuttle for nearly ninety seconds — a perfect window for the final approach.

Ghost run. The crew threads every gap, exploits every blind spot, and completes the download without a single alarm. The Empire won't know the nav data was accessed until the shuttle's next scheduled diagnostic — hours after the crew is in hyperspace.

scenes.title: The Banshee
scenes.readAloud:
Maya banks the Banshee hard as you clear Jakku's atmosphere, the desert world shrinking behind you. She's already plotting the jump — not to a standard hyperspace lane, but to what she calls the Smuggler's Path, a stitched-together chain of scavenger trails, shadow-port routes, and poorly maintained back-lanes that only the desperate or the skilled attempt.

"The Empire patrols the main lanes out of Arkanis Sector," she says, not looking up from the nav computer. "Hydian Way, Corellian Run — every checkpoint from here to the Core is Imperial. We go the long way. Four jumps, four dropouts. Each one, we recalculate."

She taps the nav display — a jagged line appears, zig-zagging northeast through the Mid Rim and Expansion Region, threading the gap between patrol corridors. "First jump takes us to a dead spot near the Trax Tube — no stations, no patrols, nothing but empty space. We recalculate there, pick up a shadow-port route through the Expansion Region, then hop to Ord Mantell for fuel and nav data. After that, one more jump to Aldhani — Imperial garrison world, so we stay in orbit just long enough to lock coordinates — then straight into the Cademimu sector."

Then she glances at the co-pilot seat — empty — and back at one of you. A half-smile. "You fly, right? Get up here. I need someone on the secondaries who knows what a yaw compensator does."

The Smuggler's Path is a nightmare of constant recalculation, blind jumps into empty space, and the ever-present risk of dropping out too close to an Imperial patrol. Maya flies with a confidence that borders on recklessness — but she's teaching as she goes, calling out readings, sharing the stick on the tight corrections. Reading the gaps between hyperspace lanes like she's done it before — and for the first time, letting someone else read them with her.

Four jumps. Four dropouts. Each one tenser than the last — the deep space recalculation where comms are dead and you're utterly alone, the white-knuckle slingshot past a gravity well near Ord Mantell, the heart-stopping moment an Imperial sensor buoy pings the Banshee near Aldhani before Maya kills the transponder and dives back into hyperspace.

When you finally drop out for the last time, the viewport fills with green. Ajan Kloss — a jungle moon orbiting a gas giant in the Cademimu Sector. And in orbit, barely visible against the planet's curve, the angular silhouette of a Victory-class Star Destroyer.
scenes.gmNotes:
Maya owns and flies the Banshee. She is the pilot for the entire campaign. This scene establishes her competence, her ship, and the co-pilot dynamic with the Ace.

CO-PILOT SEAT: Maya invites whoever has piloting skill (ideally the party's Ace Pilot) to sit co-pilot. This is NOT a test — it's a genuine invitation born from practicality and the beginnings of trust. She teaches them to read the Path, calls out corrections, shares the stick on tight maneuvers. This is the Ace Pilot's first spotlight moment. If no one has piloting skill, Maya handles it solo but comments that she could use a co-pilot — planting the seed.

BONDING MOMENT: The Smuggler's Path run is a crucible. Maya and the co-pilot are working in sync under pressure — and Maya lets her guard down. She stops performing the 'cool smuggler' act and becomes someone focused, skilled, and genuinely collaborative. This is the first real human connection she makes with the crew.

THE SMUGGLER'S PATH: A stitched-together chain of scavenger trails, shadow-port routes, and poorly maintained back-lanes that avoids Imperial patrols. Maya has run variations of it before — she's a smuggler, and routes like this are how the Outer Rim moves contraband. The route requires four separate hyperspace jumps with manual recalculation at each dropout point:

JUMP 1: Jakku (I-13) → Deep Space Dropout (~J-12). Exit scavenger trails into empty space near the Trax Tube corridor. No stations, no patrols — just dead space. Recalculate to pick up shadow-port routes heading coreward.

JUMP 2: Deep Space → Expansion Region Gap (~K-9). Threading between patrol corridors through the Mid Rim. Drop out in the gap between the Lesser Lantillian Route and the Corellian Trade Spine. Recalculate for the run to Ord Mantell.

JUMP 3: Expansion Region → Ord Mantell (L-7). Refuel at the junkyard bazaars. Buy fresh nav data for the Cademimu sector from black-market astrogators. The crew has a few hours here — enough to resupply or get into trouble.

JUMP 4: Ord Mantell → Aldhani (M-6). Imperial garrison world in the Cademimu sector. Maya drops out just long enough to lock final coordinates for the Ajara system, then punches it before Imperial sensors can get a clean read.

FINAL JUMP: Aldhani → Ajan Kloss (L-5). Short jump into the Ajara system. Arrive at the jungle moon.

The Ace co-pilot makes real contributions at each dropout: calling out gravity shadows, adjusting deflector angles, managing power distribution during recalculation windows.

AJAN KLOSS APPROACH: Upon arrival, the heroes detect a Victory-class Star Destroyer in orbit and V-wing patrols. The Vanishing Place is on the surface. Landing must avoid Imperial detection — Maya identifies a canyon approach that masks their signature from orbital sensors.

NARRATIVE FUNCTION: This scene transitions from Part 1 to Part 2. It establishes:
1. Maya as the crew's pilot and ship owner
2. The co-pilot dynamic — the Ace is not a passenger, they're crew
3. The Banshee as the party's transport
4. The Imperial military presence at Ajan Kloss
5. The urgency — Varth is being held at the Vanishing Place and the Empire is about to take custody

BEAT 2 CONVERSATION HOOK: The mid-transit galley scene (Beat 2) is a structured social conversation, not freeform RP. From the GM Command Bridge, open the Conversation panel and launch [maya-banshee-galley]. Players use the Conversation overlay to queue questions; you deliver Maya's scripted responses one beat at a time. Maya starts at Comfort 4, lower than Varth's 5 — she's guarded, she gives short answers, and probe questions cost comfort. The recalc clock built into the scene gives you a clean exit lever. Run this conversation BEFORE The Crash so the players land on Ajan Kloss with Maya as a character they actually know.

encounters.name: Beat 1 — Departure & First Jump
encounters.trigger: Banshee clears Jakku atmosphere
encounters.description: Maya banks hard out of Jakku's gravity well and locks the first jump on the nav board. She glances at the empty co-pilot seat, then at whoever in the party has piloting skill (the Ace by default). "Get up here. I need someone on the secondaries who knows what a yaw compensator does." The Ace takes the seat. Maya teaches as she preps the jump — calling out the nav harmonics, the deflector pre-trim, the manual recalc points she's queued. The first jump punches in clean.

encounters.trigger: Second dropout, ~11 minutes of recalc dead-time before the next jump
encounters.description: The autopilot holds the Banshee in dead space while Maya queues the next jump. She comes aft to the galley for caf — and for the first time on this trip she's not actively flying anything. She invites the crew to ask what they're going to ask. "I won't be in a talking mood once we drop out at Aldhani. Now's the time." This is a structured social scene — the Maya conversation overlay. Launch it here: [conversation:maya-banshee-galley]
encounters.tactics: GM ACTION: Open the Conversation panel in the Command Bridge and launch [maya-banshee-galley]. Players ask questions through the player overlay; GM delivers Maya's responses one beat at a time. Maya starts at Comfort 4. The recalc clock is a built-in timer — the GM can call "two minutes left" to wind the scene down naturally. Mirrors the Varth debrief structure but tighter, terser, more guarded. End the scene when the recalc clock hits zero or comfort drops to 1.

encounters.name: Beat 3 — The Aldhani Sensor Buoy
encounters.trigger: Third dropout — Aldhani system, near Imperial garrison world
encounters.description: The Banshee drops out of hyperspace closer to Aldhani than Maya wanted — a recalc misalignment. An Imperial sensor buoy pings the ship within ninety seconds. Maya kills the transponder, the Ace adjusts deflector angles to mask the heat signature, and somebody on a third station (Sensors/Comms) needs to spoof the buoy's return ping before it phones home.
encounters.tactics: Tense ~90-second window. Piloting check (Hard) by the Ace OR a Tech check (Hard) on the comms station to spoof the buoy. Either succeeds. Failure = the buoy logs a Banshee signature; an Imperial patrol will be looking for them in the next sector — escalate the Aldhani garrison's interest in subsequent adventures. Mastery = clean spoof, plus they pull the buoy's patrol schedule and gain advantage on the next Smuggler's Path traversal.

encounters.name: Beat 4 — Ord Mantell Slingshot
encounters.trigger: Fourth dropout — gravity shadow near Ord Mantell
encounters.description: Maya plots a gravity-assist slingshot around an Ord Mantell moon to shave eighteen minutes off the next jump's calc time. The maneuver requires precise throttle work in the upper atmosphere — too steep and they skip off, too shallow and the gravity well drags them in. Optional: anyone hot to try the gunwell can drop down and run a target-drone calibration on the ventral turret while Maya pulls the slingshot, working out the kinks Maya hasn't had time to test since the last refit.
encounters.tactics: Piloting check (Average) by Maya — automatic success unless the GM wants drama. Real spotlight: any crew member who wants to volunteer for gunwell duty can run a Gunnery + Tech assist that calibrates the turret for Adventure 1's later combat (preview/familiarization moment with the ventral turret station). Optional sabacc-deck downtime in the common room for non-crew players — pure flavor, no mechanics.

encounters.name: Beat 5 — Ajan Kloss, Final Approach Setup
encounters.trigger: Fifth and final dropout — Cademimu sector, Ajara system edge
encounters.description: The viewport fills with green. Ajan Kloss — a jungle moon orbiting a gas giant. And in orbit, just visible against the planet's curve, the angular silhouette of a Victory-class Star Destroyer. Maya identifies a canyon approach that will mask the Banshee from orbital sensors. The Ace locks the approach vector. Maya hands the stick over: "You've earned the seat. Take us in." Hard cut to The Crash.
encounters.tactics: No dice — narrative pivot beat. The Ace is now flying. The next scene (The Crash) opens with them at the controls, descending into the canyon, when the perimeter defense turrets open up. This is the moment the Banshee transitions from 'Maya's ship' to 'the crew's ship' — at least for the next ten minutes.
